newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Jailed rebel could hold key to Timor future.
newsitem.headline: Jailed rebel could hold key to Timor future.

text.p: East Timorese rebel leader Jose "Xanana" Gusmao, languishing in a Jakarta jail for opposing Indonesia's rule of the troubled territory, could hold the key to its future.

On Wednesday, South African President Nelson Mandela added his voice to the chorus of appeals for Gusmao's freedom. He said after a meeting with Portuguese President Jorge Sampaio that no solution to the problems of East Timor was possible until all its leaders, including Gusmao, were free.
A poet who once studied in a Jesuit seminary, Gusmao was the leader of a dwindling band of armed guerrillas until his capture in 1992.

He is currently serving a 20-year sentence in Jakarta's Cipinang prison for his relentless battle against Indonesia's December 1975 invasion of East Timor and its annexation of the mainly-Catholic territory the following year.

Gusmao has long been a sticking point between Indonesia and Portugal, East Timor's former colonial ruler. Lisbon has insisted he be released to improve the chance of worthwhile progress in negotiations on the future of the territory and Jakarta has so far refused.
Gusmao has remained steadfastly in the limelight despite his incarceration; indeed his stature appears to have grown in recent months.
When his spokesman in exile, Jose Ramos-Horta, was jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize last year, he said Gusmao was a more deserving candidate.

Mandela asked for and received permission to meet him while on a state visit to Indonesia in mid-July and Gusmao was taken from jail for dinner with the South African president at the state guest house.
Earlier this year, Gusmao also met Jamsheed Marker, the U.N. special envoy for East Timor.

Born in the East Timorese town of Mana Luto on June 20, 1946, Gusmao is the second son in a family of nine children. He studied for four years at a Jesuit seminary in Dare, in the hills overlooking the provincial capital Dili, and also attended Dili High School.
He did three years compulsory service in the colonial Portuguese forces and later worked in the local government department of the colonial administration.
He married in October 1969. His wife, Emilia, and their two children now live in Melbourne, Australia. Gusmao has not seen his family since 1975.
In 1974, he won East Timor's poetry prize for a poem called "Mauberedias," inspired by famed Portuguese poet Luis De Camoes's epic "Lusadias".
He moved to Australia later that year and became involved with East Timor's Fretilin party, which was coming into its own as Portugal began to decolonise its territorial possessions.
Gusmao left Australia in November 1975, travelling to his homeland a week before the invasion by Indonesian troops.

He remained to join armed opposition to Indonesia, and took over Fretilin's military wing in 1978. In the period until his capture, he led an ill-equipped band of guerrillas against Indonesia's vastly superior forces, becoming almost a legend among the people of East Timor.

Although accused of taking part in executions and massacres, Gusmao is also known for negotiating a three-month ceasefire with Indonesian troops in 1983 which triggered a schism in the guerrilla movement.

After his capture, Indonesia gave wide publicity to his trial, but it bordered on farce as a witness called to speak against him shouted slogans of support before being dragged from the courtroom. Gusmao himself was barred from reading a defence statement.
After he was initially sentenced to life imprisonment, the term was reduced to 20 years in 1993.
As pressure for his release mounted, Ramos-Horta asserted that Gusmao would not accept freedom if it meant he had to go into exile.
Gusmao has said he supports U.N. Secretary-General Koffi Annan's initiatives on East Timor.
"I believe that Koffi Annan will fulfil his commitment to East Timor," Gusmao said in a radio interview smuggled out of prison and broadcast on Portuguese radio station Renascenca in July.
"The steps he has taken so far are more encouraging than in recent years."
